blocks.text: **Linux** is a family of **open-source, Unix-like** operating systems built around the **Linux kernel**. It follows Unix design principles but was developed independently. Linux is classed as **open-source system software**.

blocks.title: Key facts
rows: The Linux kernel uses the **GNU GPL version 2** licence

blocks.title: What open source means here
items: Source code may be studied, modified and redistributed under its licence.
Many distributions are free to obtain, but paid support and services also exist.
A **distribution** packages the kernel with utilities, applications and installation tools.

blocks.text: 'Linux distribution' is a **category** of products, not Linux's original name. A distribution contains more than the kernel alone.

blocks.title: Key features
rows: Separate accounts can use system resources
Choose your software, desktops and system settings
Valued for stability, security controls and flexibility

blocks.title: Interfaces and languages
rows: Mainly **C**, plus assembly and support for Rust

blocks.title: Security fact check
blocks.text: Linux **can be affected by malware** - it is not virus-proof. End-to-end encryption belongs to specific apps and protocols, not to all Linux activity.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: Torvalds - 1991 - Unix-like - Open source - Multi-user - Multitasking.
A **Linux distribution** (distro) combines the kernel, utilities, package management and other software into a ready-to-install system.

blocks.title: Distribution and what it is known for
rows: Stability and reliability, especially Debian Stable
Debian-based; developed by **Canonical** with community contributions
**Red Hat Enterprise Linux** - designed for business and enterprise workloads and servers
Community Linux project **sponsored by Red Hat**
Distinguish historical CentOS Linux from CentOS Stream
Flexible system with strong source-based customisation
Community distribution for desktop and server use

blocks.title: High-value pairs
blocks.text: Ubuntu = Debian-based = Canonical. Fedora = Red Hat. RHEL = enterprise. SUSE = Germany. Debian = stability. Kali = security testing.

sections.title: Kali Linux, other names, GNOME and GNU

blocks.title: Kali Linux
rows: Built for authorised **penetration testing**, security auditing and digital forensics

blocks.title: Other names that appear in exams
items: Slackware, KNOPPIX, Mandriva, MEPIS and Xandros.
Some of these are historical distributions.
Novell was a company associated with SUSE.

blocks.title: Desktop and GNU
rows: One desktop environment; originally meant 'GNU Network Object Model Environment'

blocks.text: GNOME is **one** desktop option, not the only Linux GUI. Linux also offers alternatives such as KDE Plasma.

rows: Central component managing CPU time, memory, processes and devices
Let the kernel communicate with hardware
Interprets commands and runs programs or scripts
Text interface through which a shell is commonly used
Shows that the shell is ready for input

items: User / applications
Types commands, runs programs
Shell

Kernel (+ drivers)

Hardware
Physical machine

blocks.text: A **kernel** is the central resource manager - it is not a shell or a text editor. Kernel manages resources, shell interprets commands.
Linux uses a **monolithic kernel with loadable modules**. The designs below are general kernel concepts - they are **not five types of Linux kernel**.

blocks.title: Kernel design concepts
rows: Most core services run in kernel space (Linux's approach)
Only essential services remain in kernel space
Gives applications more control of the allocated resources

blocks.text: Linux is **monolithic** (with loadable modules). Do not choose microkernel, hybrid, nanokernel or exokernel for Linux.

blocks.title: Important locations
rows: Typical home of an ordinary user
Usual home of the root account

blocks.title: File-name rules
items: Names beginning with a dot, such as .profile, are normally hidden.
Names are generally case-sensitive.
Many resources have file-like interfaces - the Unix 'everything is a file' principle.

blocks.text: The **root user** (administrative account) and the **root directory** (/) are different concepts.

blocks.title: Navigation
rows: Prints the current working directory's path

blocks.title: Directories and files
rows: Moves a file into the notes directory
Creates an empty file if it does not exist; also updates timestamps of an existing file

blocks.title: Text, help and permissions
rows: Displays file contents; cat also concatenates files
Opens the available manual page for cp
Adds execute permission for the owner

blocks.text: **touch** does not only create files - it can also **update timestamps** of an existing file.

sections.title: Output redirection and command memory aids

blocks.title: Output redirection
rows: Writes the output to files.txt, **replacing** existing contents

blocks.text: Both operators can create the target file if it does not already exist. Remember: **>** overwrites, **>>** appends.

blocks.title: Where am I? Command memory aid
Mini practice
items: pwd - shows the starting location.
mkdir linux_notes - creates a directory.
cd linux_notes - enters the directory.
touch revision.txt - creates an empty file.
ls - lists its contents.

blocks.title: Process commands
rows: Continuously updating view of processes and resources
Sends a signal to a process; by default requests termination

blocks.title: Virtual memory and swap
items: Linux supports **virtual memory** and per-process virtual address spaces.
**Swap** stores memory pages moved out of RAM.
Disk-backed swap may use a file or a partition and is **slower than RAM**.
Compressed RAM-based swap also exists.

blocks.text: **ps** gives a snapshot, while **top** updates its display continuously. **kill** sends signals; it does not always forcibly terminate. Swap is not equal in speed to physical RAM.

blocks.title: Booting
rows: **GRand Unified Bootloader** - widely used, but Linux supports other bootloaders

blocks.title: File systems
rows: **Fourth Extended File System** - widely used on Linux
Scalable journaling file system; use the name XFS rather than a misleading expansion
Copy-on-write file system with snapshots and checksums; often called B-tree FS or Butter FS

blocks.text: ext4 is common, but **no file system is the default for all Linux installations** - defaults vary by distribution. GRUB is common, not the only bootloader.

rows: Schedules or starts an **orderly** shutdown - the general shutdown command
Halts the system; power-off depends on implementation and options

blocks.title: Corrected exam answer
blocks.text: **stop** is not a standard general shutdown command. So a question listing shutdown, halt, poweroff and 'stop' cannot have 'all of these' as the answer - the general shutdown command is **shutdown**.
Remember the trio: **shutdown** (orderly), **poweroff** (shut down and power off), **halt** (stop the system).

blocks.title: Important distinctions
items: A kernel is the central resource manager, not a shell or a text editor.
Linux is not immune to malware.
The root account is not the root directory.
GNOME is one desktop option, not the only Linux GUI.

revision: Linux kernel creator: Linus Torvalds; first kernel release 0.01 on 17 September 1991; mascot Tux the penguin.
Linux is open-source, Unix-like system software; the kernel uses the GNU GPL version 2 licence.
A distribution = kernel plus utilities, applications and package management.
Ubuntu = Debian-based, by Canonical; Fedora = sponsored by Red Hat; RHEL = enterprise; SUSE = Germany.
Debian is known for stability; Kali Linux is for authorised penetration testing (Mati Aharoni, Devon Kearns).
Kernel manages CPU, memory, processes and devices; shell interprets commands; Linux has a monolithic kernel.
Root directory = /; root user = superuser; they are different. /home is for users, /dev for devices, /etc for configuration.
Permissions r, w, x for owner, group and others; chmod changes them.
pwd = current path, cd = change directory, ls = list, mkdir = create directory, cp = copy, mv = move or rename, rm = remove.
man opens manual pages; cat displays or joins files; grep searches text; touch creates a file or updates timestamps.
> overwrites a file with output; >> appends output to it.
ps = process snapshot, top = live view, kill = sends a signal, df = disk space, free = memory and swap.
Swap is slower than RAM; GRUB = GRand Unified Bootloader; ext4 is common but no universal default file system.
General shutdown command is shutdown; 'stop' is not a standard shutdown command.
GNU = GNU's Not Unix; GNOME is only one desktop environment; Linux can be hit by malware.
